title: Does polarized training improve performance in recreational runners?
authors: Munoz I, Seiler S, Bautista J, Espana J, Larumbe E, Esteve-Lanao J
journal: International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance
population: Recreational endurance runners, 10-week HR-controlled intervention, 10 km race outcome
findings: 30 runners randomised to polarized (about 77/3/20 time in zones 1/2/3) or between-thresholds (about 46/35/19) training for 10 weeks.
Both groups improved 10 km time: 39:18 to 37:19 (polarized, P<.0001) and 39:24 to 38:00 (between-thresholds, P<.001); improvements 5.0% vs 3.6%, about 41 s difference, not significant.
Post-hoc subset of the runners who actually performed the most polarized (n=6) and between-thresholds (n=16) distributions: 1.29 effect-size units in favour of polarized (90% CI 0.31-2.27, P=.038).
limitations: Primary between-group difference was not significant; the positive finding is a post-hoc subset with unequal tiny groups. Ten weeks only. Authors' conclusion that polarized 'can stimulate greater training effects' is stronger than the primary result.
implications: Both distributions improved recreational 10 km times in 10 weeks, so the evidence does not justify rigid insistence on polarization for recreational runners.
Where execution is adherent, favour a low-intensity-dominant layout (about 75-80% zone 1) over a large zone 2 block, but label the evidence weak.
Surface executed versus planned TID to the user, because the post-hoc effect depended on what runners actually did.
